catalog_quote: 2.3 Pitch-accent. Many of the non-Austronesian languages of western Irian Jaya are said to be pitch-accent languages (Donohue 1997). Meyah also appears to be a pitch-accent language. It uses two phonemic pitch levels [+HIGH] and [-HIGH], as shown in (1) and (2). Contrast between [+HIGH] and [-HIGH] syllables on monosyllabic roots is shown in (1). (1) éj 'drink' èj peel; mós fish mòs toad; ót wash òt stand; óf close òf sing. Contrast between accented syllables on polysyllabic roots. (2) éfès young èfés fat; ésmà receive èsmá fallen; éfèn trim èfén possess; érèrà spicy érèrá hug; òfóká river mouth òfòká name. There are a small number of polysyllabic word roots with two, or in some cases, three accented syllables. Some of the accented syllables are adjacent to one another, others are not, as shown in (3). tone_statements.citation: Reesink, Ger P. 2002. The eastern Bird's Head languages compared. In Ger P. Reesink (ed.), Languages of the eastern Bird's Head, 1-44. Pacific Linguistics 524. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University.
tone_statements.quote: All EBH languages have a five-vowel system: i, e, a, o, u. ... Fricatives are present, either as phonemes ... or as allophones. Mpur clearly has phonemic tone, Meyah and Sougb a pitch-accent system. Hatam and Mansim do not have a tonal distinction, which they may well have had in the past (the number of homophones in Hatam is considerable), but Hatam does have a very pronounced iambic stress pattern over the utterance as a whole, defying attempts to determine a pattern of word stress.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 7.1 'Phonology', p. 26; cf. sec. 4.8, p. 18 for the high/low tone pair
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Meyah characterised as pitch accent (not full lexical tone); a high vs low pitch contrast on monosyllables is reported second-hand from Gravelle; no inventory, TBU or rules given - defers to Gravelle's chapter in the same volume.

sources.quote: 'Meyah is a pitch accent language. tone.says: The 1991 phonology treats Meah word prosody purely as phonemic STRESS, with no mention of tone, pitch or accent anywhere in the 36 pages (tone appears only in two cited titles in the references, Crofts 1976 and Pike & Scott 1975 on Fore pitch accent). Sec. 2 'Prosodic features' consists solely of 2.1 'Stress' (p. 2, p. 14): 'Stress is phonemic as shown by the contrast in the following word classes.' followed by stress minimal pairs between and across word classes, e.g. /'aha/ 'place' vs /a'ha/…
